clinicalPearls: Caused by the intracellular bacterium Klebsiella granulomatis (formerly Calymmatobacterium granulomatis) and acquired mainly through sexual contact, with a long and variable incubation period; classically endemic in scattered tropical and subtropical regions
The hallmark lesion is a painless, slowly progressive, beefy-red ulcer with a friable granulation-tissue base that bleeds readily on contact
Involves the genital and inguinal skin most often; a subcutaneous granulomatous groin swelling (pseudobubo) may mimic, but is not, true suppurative lymphadenopathy
Several clinical variants are described, including ulcerogranulomatous, hypertrophic, necrotic, and sclerotic forms
Diagnosis rests on demonstrating Donovan bodies, the intracytoplasmic organisms seen within large mononuclear cells on a crush smear or biopsy stained with Giemsa or Wright stain
The organism is fastidious and difficult to culture, so diagnosis is largely clinical supported by microscopy, with molecular testing used where available

Prolonged antibiotic therapy (for example azithromycin or doxycycline, with macrolide or co-trimoxazole alternatives) is continued until lesions have fully re-epithelialised, and relapse can occur weeks to months later
Partner notification and screening for co-existing sexually transmitted infections, including HIV and syphilis, are essential parts of management
reference.pathophysiology: Granuloma inguinale is a chronic, indolent genital ulcerative disease produced by the encapsulated intracellular bacterium Klebsiella granulomatis. Following sexual (and occasionally close non-sexual) contact, the organism invades and multiplies within mononuclear phagocytes of the genital and perineal skin, where it appears as clusters of Donovan bodies. The infected macrophages drive a chronic granulomatous inflammatory response with vascular proliferation, producing the characteristic friable, beefy-red ulcer that enlarges slowly by direct extension and autoinoculation. Because inflammation is subcutaneous rather than nodal, groin swelling reflects granulomatous tissue rather than true lymphadenitis, and long-standing disease can lead to fibrosis, lymphatic obstruction with genital lymphoedema, and destructive scarring.
additionalDifferentials: Chancroid caused by Haemophilus ducreyi (painful ulcer)
Squamous cell carcinoma of the genitalia
Cutaneous amoebiasis or other tropical ulcerative infection
additionalInvestigations: Tissue crush smear or punch biopsy stained with Giemsa or Wright stain to identify Donovan bodies
Histopathology of biopsy to confirm granulomatous inflammation and exclude malignancy
Polymerase chain reaction or molecular assay for Klebsiella granulomatis where available
Syphilis serology together with dark-field microscopy to exclude a chancre
HIV testing and screening for other sexually transmitted infections
Nucleic acid amplification testing for gonorrhoea and chlamydia and, where relevant, testing to exclude chancroid
redFlags: Extensive tissue destruction or genital mutilation from advanced disease
Secondary bacterial infection with spreading cellulitis or systemic sepsis
A chronic non-healing lesion raising suspicion of malignant transformation
Rare haematogenous dissemination to bone, joints, or viscera
reference.prognosis: With early and adequately prolonged antibiotic treatment lesions heal well and the outlook is good, but delayed therapy risks progressive tissue destruction, scarring, and genital lymphoedema; relapse can follow apparently successful treatment, so follow-up until complete healing is advised.
pitfalls: Assuming a painless genital ulcer is syphilis and omitting microscopy for Donovan bodies
Stopping antibiotics once the ulcer looks improved rather than continuing until full re-epithelialisation, allowing relapse
Overlooking concurrent HIV or other sexually transmitted infection
Failing to biopsy a chronic non-healing ulcer to exclude malignant change
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
BASHH UK national guideline for the management of donovanosis
CDC Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines
management: Treat with prolonged antibiotic therapy active against Klebsiella granulomatis, a macrolide (azithromycin) being first-line, with doxycycline, co-trimoxazole or erythromycin as alternatives
Continue antibiotics until the lesions have completely re-epithelialised, as therapy shorter than full healing risks relapse
Add a parenteral aminoglycoside such as gentamicin where lesions respond slowly or in immunocompromised or pregnant patients
Test for HIV and screen for coexisting sexually transmitted infections including syphilis, gonorrhoea and chlamydia
Notify and treat recent sexual contacts to prevent reinfection and onward transmission
Consider surgical intervention for extensive tissue destruction, scarring or genital lymphoedema from long-standing disease
Follow up until complete healing is confirmed, as relapse can occur after apparently successful treatment
Manage within a genitourinary medicine service with contact tracing and safe-sex counselling
